𝗩𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗢𝗥 𝗣𝗥𝗜𝗠𝗘 | Engineer Beyond Limits

We are a multidisciplinary team participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge in Cairo.

𝗢𝘂𝗿 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁: MISSION FORGE

An interactive space mission design game combining spacecraft engineering, resource management, and mission simulation.

𝗢𝘂𝗿 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻: Making space exploration engaging through scientific thinking, creative problem-solving, and engineering-driven decisions.

𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻. 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿.
summary: Horus is a browser-based game where players design a complete lunar science mission and then run it as Flight Director. Players choose a scientific objective (South Pole ice mapping, landing-site imaging, or lunar magnetic-field mapping) and design a spacecraft under real engineering constraints: mass, power, data, communications, budget, and delta-v. After a design review, they launch. During flight, timed crises such as solar flares, fuel leaks, and antenna failures test those design choices, and a post-mission report explains why the mission succeeded or failed and links it to a similar real NASA mission. A sandbox mode, a 100-run Monte Carlo simulation, and side-by-side design comparison help players explore trade-offs. The game runs offline in the browser with an Arabic and English interface. It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by showing that every engineering decision has consequences, and that failure is a way to learn.
details:
Engineering model (simplified for education)
Delta-v uses the Tsiolkovsky equation. Power compares array output against load, and battery energy must cover eclipse. Data is limited by downlink capacity and reduced by power or orbit shortfalls. Mission lifetime trades more science return against fuel, wear, operating cost, and failure risk. A separate planar Earth-Moon simulation was used to sanity-check injection (about 3.15 km/s) and capture (about 0.6 to 0.9 km/s).

Benefits and intended impact
Players learn that there is rarely one perfect design, that trade-offs are real, and that failure is a way to learn. The sandbox mode, 100-run Monte Carlo simulation, and side-by-side comparison of up to six saved designs let beginners and students experiment freely. A team mode lets four players each own one segment, mirroring real mission roles.

Creativity
Design choices matter twice: they set the mission’s limits, and they change the odds of the crises later. The game combines cinematic 3D visuals, procedurally generated audio, and an Arabic and English interface in a single offline package.

Tools
JavaScript, HTML/CSS, WebGL through three.js r128 (MIT), Web Audio API, Web Speech API, Canvas/SVG, localStorage. Testing used headless Chromium automation and a Monte Carlo simulation of tens of thousands of crisis runs to tune difficulty.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)
[Team: confirm this section matches what you actually did.] Manus was used to help formulate the engineering dimensions and equations. Anthropic’s Claude was used as a coding assistant for parts of the game code and for the Arabic/English language layer. An optional “Explain with AI” button asks Claude to explain a mission report; it works only when the game runs inside claude.ai, and a rule-based explanation is always shown. Images, 3D models, music, and voices are not SI-generated: music and effects are produced in code, and voices come from the browser’s text-to-speech.

Limitations
Engineering values are simplified, and the orbit model was not validated with GMAT. Difficulty was tuned by simulation on the crisis layer; the design layer has not had human playtesting. The English translation is partial: some design-part descriptions and report details are still in Arabic.

NASA resources
NASA Space Apps challenge page, “Design and Develop Science Missions,” Mission Design Lab, Webb “Build It Yourself,” and the Saturn V model from NASA 3D Resources.
